segments: 63. Thirty-eighth [kingdom]: of the Romans. His uncle made him king.
He, while in Athens under the name of eloquence, was learning sorcery.
And when his uncle died,
and the kingdom of the Romans came to him in his time,
he became brutish, and relied (and trusted) upon his good fortune.
And he believed that, as he claimed, the demons had exalted him.
And he began to open the idol temples,
and to sacrifice.
And he conducted himself in the false guise of philosophers,
driving away cooks, and barbers, and scribes {OCR?}.
Yet his mouth was wide open to mockery,
and his tongue prompt to derision.
And when he entered Constantinople, he was proclaimed Autocrat.
And in Antioch, when he entered and lowered the prices of everything that was sold,
he was despised by the Antiochenes,
who were easily agitated,
and they mocked his beard because it was long.
And when he wished to destroy them,
Libanius the Sophist presented a speech of supplication on their behalf.
The king, however, reviled them with words,
and assuaged his anger.
And the wicked man set up two tables:
on one was gold,
and on the other incense and fire.
And whoever wanted gold
would place incense on the fire and burn it before the idol,
and then take the gold.
Moreover, he dismissed the eunuchs, and also the camels, the donkeys, and the pack-mules from his service,
and left only the horses.
And he enacted a law that Christians should not read philosophical books.
And he established houses for the support of orphans, widows, and the poor,
and under this guise he deceived the simple-minded.
And he sent word to the Edessenes to receive him.
And when they did not receive him,
he left them and crossed over to Harran.
And he sacrificed to the idols and honored the Jews.
And when the Christians in Edessa heard this,
they were moved with zeal and killed all the Jews who were among them.
Julian, however, while divining and taking omens everywhere,
obtained an oracle saying:
"Behold, I, Ares, go before you to assist you."
And as he placed his trust [in it], he set out {OCR?}
for Persia, having with him three hundred and ninety-five thousand warriors.
And he took captives and devastated Seleucia and Ctesiphon.
And Shapur the Persian sent him a petition,
that he might give him a small portion of his territory,
and take the rest;
but he did not accept (agree. Then fierce battle was joined between the Romans and the Persians on the banks of the Tigris
